one_liner: Minimal multi-threaded epoll/kqueue HTTP/1.1 server core for Nim; about 7% above actix-web at 256-512 connections on hello-world.
what_it_does: A pure-Nim HTTP/1.1 server library. You pass a single `onRequest(req: Request): Future[void]` callback to `run()`, read `req.httpMethod`, `req.path`, `req.headers` and `req.body` (each an Option parsed on demand), and answer once with `req.send(code, body, headers)`. There is no routing, TLS, middleware, HTTP/2 or WebSocket layer; the README says to use Jester (built on httpbeast) unless you are writing your own framework or something resource-constrained. It is not a drop-in for actix-web: different language and a far lower-level, single-callback API.
how_it_is_fast: Thread-per-core, shared-nothing: with --threads:on every thread opens its own listening socket with SO_REUSEPORT and runs its own Nim `selectors` loop (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS), so the kernel spreads accepts and no connection crosses threads. Reads are non-blocking until EAGAIN; end of headers is detected by checking only the last four bytes for CRLFCRLF, with a full scan only for body-carrying methods, and method/path/headers are parsed lazily from the raw buffer when the handler asks. Responses are copied straight into a per-connection send queue by a macro-unrolled append, the Date header is cached and refreshed by a one-second timer, TCP_NODELAY is set, and a handler may return a nil Future to skip asyncdispatch entirely. HTTP pipelining is supported for bodiless requests.
when_to_use: You are writing a Nim web framework or a resource-constrained Nim service and want the raw HTTP/1.1 core that Jester and the Nim Forum run on.
Small plaintext/JSON endpoints on Linux (or macOS) behind nginx or another reverse proxy that terminates TLS and sanitizes requests.
Many keep-alive connections at moderate-to-high concurrency (256-512) where aggregate req/s matters more than tail latency.
Mostly synchronous handlers that can return a nil Future, or async handlers whose awaits are fd-based (sockets, addTimer).
when_not_to_use: Directly on the open internet: the README says it is not hardened and should sit behind a reverse proxy; a 2023 request-smuggling report (#95) was closed with that same advice, a body longer than its Content-Length trips an assertion (#21, open; with assertions off the connection waits forever), and a GET with a body is never answered (#18, open) because only POST/PUT/PATCH/CONNECT get a body scan.
Tail-latency-sensitive services: in the same 2026-09-24 run httpbeast's p99 was 8.1/10.9/11.3 ms at 64/256/512 connections vs actix-web's 0.40/1.58/3.22 ms, even though its median was lower.
You need TLS (#11, open since 2018), HTTP/2, streamed or chunked request bodies (#74, open), built-in WebSockets, or Windows (unsupported by design).
Nim 2 default ORC memory management with threads: random segfaults are reported (#80 open; #90 SIGSEGV on Nim 2.0 with Jester), and the benchmark itself builds with --mm:refc.
Large request bodies: reads go through a 256-byte stack buffer copied byte by byte into the connection string, and a user reported Vert.x faster with bodies over about 500 bytes (#86, open).

integration.form: module (Nimble package; about 720 lines of pure Nim source compiled into your program)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the Nim stdlib (selectors, asyncdispatch, net, posix); asynctools only for its tests
integration.min_toolchain: httpbeast.nimble says nim >= 0.18.0; CI tests Nim 1.4.8 and a Nim devel commit; code has a Nim 2 branch; benchmarked on Nim 2.2 with --mm:refc
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll) and macOS (kqueue), CI on ubuntu-latest and macOS-latest; no Windows by design; multi-threading needs SO_REUSEPORT (where it is missing, as on WSL, it prints that it will not use all threads)
integration.thread_safety: One selector and event loop per thread; a Request belongs to the thread and connection that produced it. `send` may be called only once per request and raises HttpBeastDefect on a stale request. The request-ID counter is a plain global incremented without atomics.

gotchas: `nimble install httpbeast` resolves to tag v0.4.1: the v0.4.2 bump (Nov 2022) and the Dec 2023 startup-callback change (PR #89, cited in #80/#90 as the ORC crash fix) are untagged, so you need `httpbeast#head` (#91 open).
The server never closes a connection after responding: it ignores `Connection: close` and HTTP/1.0 semantics, so ApacheBench (`ab`) hangs (#16, open).

Timers created with `sleepAsync` do not wake the event loop (it waits on its own selector with no timeout), so `await sleepAsync(10)` capped a benchmark at ~100 req/s; fd-based `addTimer` fixed it (#84).
The `headers` argument of `send` is spliced in raw; a trailing or embedded blank CRLF shifts the body so Content-Length no longer matches (#56, open).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick httpbeast only when the service is written in Nim or you are building a Nim framework. In the same run may_minihttp (194k req/s at 512) and fulmine.js (204k) were faster and http.zig (171k) was comparable, so in Rust, JavaScript or Zig use those instead.
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks develop-branch run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364), httpbeast 0.4 built with Nim 2.2, --mm:refc, -d:release and LTO served 179k and 176k req/s at 256 and 512 keep-alive connections vs actix-web 4.8 (Rust 1.98, LTO) at 168k and 163k (1.07x), but was 7% slower at 64 connections (167k vs 179k). Each server was pinned to 4 cores of an undisclosed 16-thread x86_64 Linux host, and each figure is the average of three hello-world routes; the same data show httpbeast's p99 3.5-20x worse than actix's.
status_note: Stale since 2023-12-10 with the last tag at v0.4.1, but MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small enough (about 720 lines) to vendor; it is still Jester's non-Windows backend.
